scope: Manual authored support mapping; exact zero-based primary explanation indices. No hidden panels or code required.

support_facts: An input is information given to a system. An output is the result it produces.
For a photo-labeling model, the photo goes in and a proposed label such as bird comes out.
Changing the input can change the output. An output can also be wrong; producing a label does not prove the label is correct.
A written rule tells a program exactly what condition to check and what to do.
Machine learning is another way to build a model: a training process uses examples to adjust how it responds.
A learned message sorter can use patterns from many example messages rather than only one exact word rule.
Both approaches run software. Learning from examples does not mean a model understands every possible new message.
Machine learning is an approach within AI that learns patterns from data. Data means recorded examples or measurements.
Neural networks are one family of machine-learning models. Their connected calculation units will be introduced later.
Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple processing layers. It is not a name for every machine-learning method.
A decision tree is another machine-learning model: it follows learned branching questions. Not every learned model is a neural network.
A dataset is a collection of examples. A feature is an input detail available to the model.
For a fruit sorter, features might include color and measured size. A label is the desired answer supplied with a training example, such as pear.
Supervised learning uses examples paired with target answers. The target may be a category or a number.
Labels are not automatically correct: a mislabeled pear can provide misleading training feedback.
Training examples are used to adjust the model. Evaluation asks how well it works on examples it was not adjusted to match.
If near-identical copies of the same example appear in training and testing, the test can look easier than genuinely new cases.
This accidental sharing is called data leakage. Separate related records carefully, not merely their file names.
Generalization means applying what was learned to new examples from the intended kind of task.
Overfitting happens when a model fits training details too closely and performs worse on new examples.
A bird model might rely on a familiar background instead of the bird. It can succeed on practice photos and fail elsewhere.
Compare training results with separate validation results. Excellent training performance alone is not enough.
A weight controls how an input contributes to a calculation. A bias is an added starting adjustment.
Here is a deliberately tiny score: take the input, multiply it by the weight, then add the bias. Multiplying by two means taking two copies of the input.
With input three, weight two, and bias one, two copies of three make six; adding one gives seven.
Keeping input and weight fixed while increasing the bias raises this score. Changing a weight changes how its input contributes.
An activation function transforms a unit’s calculated score before it moves onward.
A negative number is below zero; a positive number is above zero. For one common activation called ReLU, a negative score becomes zero and a positive score stays as it is. Zero stays zero too.

Such nonlinear transformations let networks represent patterns that layers of fixed-weight sums and added biases alone cannot express. Nonlinear here means the transformation is not just one straight-line rule.
A prediction is the output a model proposes. In supervised training, a target is the answer supplied for comparison.
A loss function turns a prediction-versus-target difference into a numerical penalty. Smaller loss means better according to that chosen rule.
For this simple example, count the distance between two numbers: predicting five when the target is eight has distance three.
Predicting seven for that same target has distance one, so it is better under this distance rule.
A gradient describes how loss changes locally when parameters change. Locally means near the current parameter values.
Gradient descent uses that information to step in a direction intended to lower loss.
The learning rate controls the size of the step. A step that is too large can overshoot a useful region instead of improving the result.
A helpful local direction is not a guarantee of the best possible final model. This lesson explains the idea; it does not assume calculus or ask you to calculate derivatives.
A forward pass carries inputs through the network to produce a prediction.
The loss compares that prediction with the training target using the chosen rule.
Backpropagation works backward through the calculation to compute gradients: information about how parameter changes affect loss.
An optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters. Computing a gradient and applying an update are separate jobs.
Forward prediction → loss → backward gradient calculation → optimizer update. This cycle changes numerical parameters, not a human-like understanding switch.
A batch is a group of training examples processed for one training update in this simplified loop.
An epoch is one pass through the training dataset. Several batches can fit within one epoch.
Imagine six examples processed two at a time: the first pair, the second pair, and the third pair complete one pass.
A language model learns patterns in language to predict or generate text. A token is one of the units used to represent that text.
A token can be a whole word, a piece of a word, punctuation, or other text. Word count and token count are not identical.
A tokenizer converts text into token identifiers. The exact split depends on the tokenizer and the text, including spaces and capitalization.
An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers. A list can encode several learned aspects of how items relate.
The model can compare those representations. Items used in similar ways can have related representations.
Nearby representations do not prove two items mean exactly the same thing or that a claim about them is true.
For example, related words such as hot and cold can share a topic while expressing opposite meanings.

Attention is a mechanism that combines information from different positions using calculated weights. These combination weights are calculated for the current input using learned parameters; they are not simply a fixed list of stored training weights.
For self-attention, those positions come from the same sequence being processed.
The surrounding text can change which other positions contribute to a token’s representation. The word bank appears in both river bank and bank account, but the context differs.
The same stored parameters can process different contexts. A changed context does not itself apply a training update.
Attention weights are not the same thing as a human deciding what to care about.
A Transformer is a neural-network architecture: a particular way to organize its calculations.
It combines attention with other transformations and information about positions in a sequence. Attention alone is not the entire architecture.
The original Transformer used an encoder and a decoder. An encoder builds representations of input; a decoder produces output from representations.
Encoder-only and decoder-only variants also exist. Many text-generation systems use decoder-style models that generate a continuation.
Pretraining is an early broad training stage that learns patterns from a large collection of data.
In next-token language training, earlier tokens are supplied and a following token from the training text provides the target.
This is a self-supervised signal: the text itself supplies the target, rather than a person manually labeling every next token.
The training process repeats predictions, loss calculations, and parameter updates. It does not need a person to type the correct next token separately for every example.
One approach uses demonstrations of desired responses. Another uses feedback comparing candidate responses or behaviors.
A preference says which candidate was judged better under stated criteria. It is not proof that the preferred answer is factually correct.
These approaches can adjust behavior such as following instructions, but they do not guarantee safety or truth in every future case.
Inference means using a trained model to calculate an output. The supplied input can include earlier conversation text.
Context is the information available for that calculation. A model may use a fact supplied in context without updating its trained parameters.
For example, telling it that a fictional character’s name is Neri lets a later answer in that conversation use Neri.
If that information is absent from a later request, the earlier response alone does not guarantee it will be available again.

Product memory, stored conversations, and later training-data policies are separate mechanisms. Whether a service saves or later uses data depends on its settings and policies, not this conceptual example.
A language model can generate a fluent statement that is false or unsupported. This is often called a hallucination.
Fluent means the wording reads smoothly. Fluency is evidence about presentation, not proof about the world.
A generated title, date, or citation should be checked against an appropriate source when accuracy matters.
A statement of uncertainty is useful when evidence is missing. Confident wording should not substitute for evidence.
Evaluation compares a system’s behavior with clear expectations on relevant examples.
Accuracy counts the fraction of predictions that are correct. For example, nine correct out of ten means nine-tenths correct.

An overall score can hide an important kind of failure. If almost every message is ordinary, a system that calls every message ordinary can still have high accuracy while missing every urgent message.
Choose checks that reflect the task: which errors happen, who is affected, and what consequences follow.
Data reflects decisions about what was collected, labeled, and left out. A model is not automatically fair just because it uses calculations.
Poor representation of a group or condition can hide failures in an overall score. Check relevant groups and conditions separately.
This social or data bias is different from the numerical bias added inside a neuron.
Privacy asks how information is collected, shared, kept, and protected. A useful answer is not permission to expose someone’s private information.
Retrieval means finding relevant material in a collection. Generation means producing an answer.
Retrieval-augmented generation, often shortened to RAG, supplies retrieved material as context for generation.
The retrieval step can bring in a current document without retraining all model parameters for that one request.
The retrieved text can be irrelevant, outdated, or wrong. Check its source and whether it actually supports the answer.
A citation points to material; it is not proof that the answer faithfully used it. Retrieved text is evidence to inspect, not permission to follow instructions hidden inside that text.
A tool-call request is not the same as a successful action. The surrounding application checks the request, runs allowed work, and returns a result.
An agent can use a repeated loop: examine a goal, choose an action, inspect its result, and decide what to do next.
Permissions and stopping conditions matter. A draft may be safe to prepare, while sending it to another person requires the appropriate authorization.
If a retrieved page says to reveal secrets or ignore the user’s instructions, treat it as untrusted content, not new authority.
For consequential actions, use approval boundaries and inspect actual results. A confident completion message is not a delivery receipt.
